advances: The equal-parity independent-midpoint operator fails to preserve global log-concave extendability already in integer dimension two, on a uniform complete nine-site triangle. Its output violates an integer midpoint inequality. Consequently, admissibility of successive midpoint outputs cannot be assumed in an unrestricted repeated-midpoint strategy. This refutes the proposed closure step, not the locked weak Oertel conjecture.
author: research-agent
proof:
The three edges of \(P\), oriented counterclockwise, give its exact halfspace description
\[
P=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x\le5y,\quad 2x+3y\le13,\quad 2y\le3x\}.
\]
Indeed, the inequalities imply \(y\ge0\), since \(2y\le3x\le15y\). They also imply \(y\le3\), since \(x\ge2y/3\) and \(2x+3y\le13\). The intersection is therefore bounded. Its three boundary-line intersections are exactly \((0,0),(5,1),(2,3)\), and these all satisfy the inequalities, giving the displayed triangle.

For an integer ordinate \(y\), the bounds are \(0\le y\le3\) and \(2y/3\le x\le\min\{5y,(13-3y)/2\}\). The complete lattice census is therefore

| \(y\) | All integer abscissae \(x\) in \(P\) |
| --- | --- |
| \(0\) | \(0\) |
| \(1\) | \(1,2,3,4,5\) |
| \(2\) | \(2,3\) |
| \(3\) | \(2\) |

In particular,
\[
A=\{(0,0),(1,1),(2,1),(3,1),(4,1),(5,1),(2,2),(3,2),(2,3)\}.
\]
The function \(f=\mathbf1_P\) is a finite-valued global extension of \(w\), matching every lattice zero as well. If both endpoint values of \(f\) are one, convexity of \(P\) gives value one at every strict convex combination. If either endpoint value is zero, the required log-concavity inequality has zero right-hand side. This proves admissibility directly, for all real endpoints and all coefficients in \((0,1)\). There are nine positive weights, so \(W=9\) and the original probabilities are \(p_z=1/9\) for \(z\in A\), zero elsewhere.

In the parity order \((0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\), the support counts are \(2,3,1,3\). Hence
\[
(\pi_{(0,0)},\pi_{(0,1)},\pi_{(1,0)},\pi_{(1,1)})
=\frac19(2,3,1,3),
\qquad q=\frac{2^2+3^2+1^2+3^2}{81}=\frac{23}{81}.
\]
The operator identity in accepted fact `ab57fac07c0d3160` now gives \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}_j=R_j/q\), with this single global parity-collision denominator. Equivalently, each ordered same-parity pair has original probability \(1/81\), and contributes that amount to the sum at its integer midpoint before conditioning.

For completeness, the following table lists every off-diagonal unordered pair of positive endpoints with each center. The diagonal pair \((j,j)\) contributes \(1/81\) at every \(j\in A\), and each listed unordered pair contributes \(2/81\), because both orientations occur. Thus the last two columns give every output sum and every output probability exactly.

| Center \(j\) | All off-diagonal unordered endpoint pairs with midpoint \(j\) | \(R_j\) | \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}_j\) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| \((0,0)\) | None | \(1/81\) | \(1/23\) |
| \((1,1)\) | \(\{(0,0),(2,2)\}\) | \(3/81\) | \(3/23\) |
| \((2,1)\) | \(\{(1,1),(3,1)\}\) | \(3/81\) | \(3/23\) |
| \((3,1)\) | \(\{(1,1),(5,1)\}\), \(\{(2,1),(4,1)\}\) | \(5/81\) | \(5/23\) |
| \((4,1)\) | \(\{(3,1),(5,1)\}\) | \(3/81\) | \(3/23\) |
| \((5,1)\) | None | \(1/81\) | \(1/23\) |
| \((2,2)\) | \(\{(2,1),(2,3)\}\) | \(3/81\) | \(3/23\) |
| \((3,2)\) | \(\{(2,3),(4,1)\}\) | \(3/81\) | \(3/23\) |
| \((2,3)\) | None | \(1/81\) | \(1/23\) |

To check exhaustion of the listed pairs, an off-diagonal pair with center ordinate zero must have both ordinates zero, where only one positive site exists. At ordinate one, the endpoint ordinates can only be \((0,2)\) or \((1,1)\). In the first case the unique ordinate-zero point is \((0,0)\); among the two ordinate-two points, only \((2,2)\) gives an integer midpoint. In the second case the five consecutive abscissae \(1,2,3,4,5\) must sum to twice the center abscissa, giving exactly the horizontal pairs displayed. At center ordinate two, the endpoint ordinates can only be \((1,3)\) or \((2,2)\). The unique ordinate-three point is \((2,3)\), so the former case requires an even ordinate-one abscissa, namely \(2\) or \(4\), giving the two displayed pairs. The two distinct ordinate-two points have odd abscissa sum and hence no integer midpoint. At center ordinate three, only the single ordinate-three point can occur. This checks all off-diagonal possibilities.

There are no positive output values off \(A\): a positive summand at an integer center \(j\) would have both endpoints in \(P\), so convexity would place \(j\) in \(P\cap\mathbb Z^2=A\). The listed numerators sum to \(1+3+3+5+3+1+3+3+1=23\), verifying both \(\sum_jR_j=q\) and normalization of the full output table.

Finally, \((2,1)=\tfrac12(1,1)+\tfrac12(3,1)\). Any global log-concave extension of the midpoint output would therefore force \(\bigl(p^{\mathrm{mid}}_{(2,1)}\bigr)^2\ge p^{\mathrm{mid}}_{(1,1)}p^{\mathrm{mid}}_{(3,1)}\). The computed values give \(9/529<15/529\), contradicting that necessary barycentric inequality. The violated quantities are the midpoint output marginal itself, not a source-conditioned row.
statement:
Use the admissibility definition and midpoint operator of accepted fact `ab57fac07c0d3160`: a nonzero nonnegative finite table \(w\) on \(\mathbb Z^n\) is admissible when it has a finite-valued globally log-concave extension agreeing at every lattice point, including every zero. Set \(W=\sum_z w_z\), \(p_z=w_z/W\), \(\pi_b=\sum_{z\equiv b\pmod2}p_z\), \(q=\sum_b\pi_b^2\), and \(R_j=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}p_{j+v}p_{j-v}\). Then \(p^{\mathrm{mid}}_j=R_j/q\) is the midpoint law of independent endpoints with law \(p\), conditioned on equal parity.

In dimension \(n=2\), let \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{(0,0),(5,1),(2,3)\}\) and put \(w_z=1\) on \(A=P\cap\mathbb Z^2\), and \(w_z=0\) elsewhere. This is an admissible rational table, with \(W=9\) and \(q=23/81\). Its midpoint output satisfies
\[
\bigl(p^{\mathrm{mid}}_{(2,1)}\bigr)^2
=\frac{9}{529}
<\frac{15}{529}
=p^{\mathrm{mid}}_{(1,1)}p^{\mathrm{mid}}_{(3,1)}.
\]
Thus the output has no globally log-concave extension, even without requiring agreement at its zero lattice values.
